## Concepts and intuitions {.unnumbered}
Everyone has checked their average grade to see if one passes of fail or get a mark, but, no one has ever check the variance of their grades!
While calculating the mean is well engrained, most probably don't remember the formula for variance or standard deviation.
But to a certain extent, we know mean is not enough, sometimes parents will look at the range of your grade (mostly the low ones).
And at the university, having 0 on one subject is failure.

In the two examples above, one is essentially looking at extremes, but why ignore all remaining information.
The variance is a statistic that is used to summarize the spread of the data,  most specifically, spread around the mean.
Why the mean is called central tendency, the variance (and the standard devitation) is a measure of dispersion.

Well, the variance is actually also an average, it is the average distance between your data and the mean. So if x1, x2, x3, x4, with mean xbar, then variance d1 = (x1 - xbar)^2, d2 = (x2 - xbar)^2, d3, and d4 and then variance is average of d1, d2, d3, d4.

Why the square? There are many explanation but the simplest is that distance needs to be positive and so squaring the numbers makes it positive. It is also for that reason that we have standard deviation as a square root of variance, so as to bring the same scale as our orgininal x1.
In other word, it allows us to interpret the value, for instance if grades are 0, 0, 20, 20, the variance is 100 which is not interpratable but a standard deviation of 10 around mean 10 makes sense.

Most data we encounter are complex, looking at movie, hotel or restaurant, ratings.
Mean is a convenient straighforward way to look at it but just the mean could be misleading (think about bi-modal distribution @sec-mode), alternatively one can look at the distribution (@sec-distribution), and intermediate approach is to look at mean and also the variance (or standard deviation) and such can improve comparison (between two distribution) and decision making.

## Formal {.unnumbered}
$$
\mathrm{Var}(X) = \sum_i (x_i - \mu)^2 \, p(x_i)
$${#eq-variance_d}

$$
\mathrm{Var}(X) = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} (x - \mu)^2 f(x)\,dx
$$ {#eq-variance_c}


Just like the mean, the definition of variance in statistics is strictly divided between applied statistics (the descriptive measure of spread computed from a physical sample) and theoretical statistics (the expected squared deviation of a random variable from its population mean).
Here are the rigorous definitions for both, complete with textbook sources and raw LaTeX formatting.
1. Applied Statistics: The Sample Variance
In applied statistics, variance is a statistic used to measure the dispersion of an observed dataset. Crucially, the rigorous definition uses a divisor of n−1 (Bessel's correction) rather than n to ensure the sample variance is an unbiased estimator of the population variance.

Publisher: Duxbury / Thomson Learning

2. Theoretical Statistics: The Population Variance
In statistical theory, the variance of a random variable X is defined as the mathematical expectation of its squared distance from its theoretical mean (μ).
Textbook Source
Book: Introduction to Mathematical Statistics (8th Edition, 2019)
Authors: Robert V. Hogg, Joseph W. McKean, and Allen T. Craig
Publisher: Pearson
The Definition
In Chapter 1 ("Probability and Distributions"), the authors define the theoretical variance (often denoted as σ
2
  or Var(X)):
"Let X be a random variable with a finite mean μ=E[X]. The variance of X, denoted by σ
2
  or Var(X), is defined by
$\sigma^2 = \operatorname{Var}(X) = \mathbb{E}[(X - \mu)^2]$
"

Depending on the underlying distribution of the variable, this expectation is evaluated using two distinct mathematical operations:
A. The Discrete Theoretical Case
If X is discrete with space D and probability mass function p(x):
$\sigma^2 = \sum_{x \in \mathcal{D}} (x - \mu)^2 p(x)$

B. The Continuous Theoretical Case
If X is continuous with probability density function f(x):
$\sigma^2 = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} (x - \mu)^2 f(x) \, dx$



1. The Theoretical "Shortcut" Formula
In textbook proofs and algebraic manipulations, the theoretical definition is frequently re-expressed using a foundational identity derived from the linearity of expectation.

Textbook Source
Book: Mathematical Statistics and Data Analysis (3rd Edition, 2007)
Author: John A. Rice
Publisher: Cengage Learning
The Definition

In Chapter 4 ("Expected Values"), Rice demonstrates the standard computational theorem for variance:
"Theorem: If X has a finite mean μ, then
$\operatorname{Var}(X) = \mathbb{E}[X^2] - (\mathbb{E}[X])^2$

That is, the variance is the expected value of the square minus the square of the expected value."

## Tips and warnings {.unnumbered}
- Variance divided by n and n-1
- squared minus mean squared
- normal dist with two parameters, if know the mean and the variance then we know the whole distribution.
- Do you compute the average of two numbers? Variance of three nunmbers?
- Sample size
